description: We're Project Solarax, and we build tools that transform complex space data into clear insights and discoveries. Our team combines software engineering, AI, and data visualization to build meaningful technology.
summary: Sky Timeline is a public web tool that plays every SPHEREx image of one patch of sky like a short film, so anyone can spot what moves or changes. Pick a spot on a 3D sky globe, type RA and Dec, search a name, or open a link with the coordinates in it. The tool finds every SPHEREx image covering that spot in NASA's IRSA archive, measures the target pixel in each, and shows them in date order. You can blink two dates, subtract or add them, view a heatmap of what changed, and read a spectrum across the six detectors. Gaia and AllWISE sources are drawn on the image, and quality flags are shown for every frame. Two small neural networks we built, BlinkNet and SpecNet, score each target as a candidate mover, variable, star or brown dwarf. The five targets named in the challenge, plus Proxima Centauri and TRAPPIST-1, are saved with the site and open instantly. It matters because finding a faint moving object, like a distant planet or a nearby brown dwarf, starts with someone noticing a dot that jumped.
details:
What it does: Sky Timeline turns SPHEREx's repeated all-sky scans into a timeline for any position. Enter coordinates in degrees or hours, click the globe or the flat map, or search an object name. The viewer plays the images as a timelapse and offers Blink, Subtract, Add and Heatmap to compare any two dates. A spectrum tab plots brightness against wavelength from every image, with filters for detectors D1 to D6. Each frame shows its flux, variance and contamination flag. Gaia DR3 and AllWISE sources are overlaid on the cutout. Coordinates live in the URL, so any view can be shared. You can save spots in your browser and download the measurements as JSON.

How it works: a Next.js site talks to a FastAPI service. The service queries NASA/IPAC IRSA (TAP first, SIA as fallback), cuts out each image with Astropy, and reads the target pixel. Saved targets ship with the site as static files, so they open in a fraction of a second. New positions are fetched live from the archive.

Neural networks: BlinkNet is a convolutional network that compares the first and last image of a target and scores settled, mover, variable or artifact. SpecNet reads the six detector fluxes and scores star, brown dwarf, galaxy or solar system body. Both were written in NumPy and trained on synthetic examples, so their labels are shown as candidates, with a warning when the label disagrees with the measured pixel shift. An optional "Explain with AI" button sends only the measured numbers to Google Gemini AI api for a simple summary.

Solar system: paths of twelve spacecraft-visited asteroids are drawn day by day from live JPL Horizons positions, and you can open the SPHEREx images along a path.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Next.js, Python, FastAPI, Astropy, PyVO, NumPy, Netlify, Render.
